_note: Hand-crafted theme mapping. Clusters 0, 3, 4 are noise and excluded.

norms-enforcement.label: Norm Enforcement & the Rules Gap
norms-enforcement.description: Students across programs identify a persistent gap between stated classroom norms and their enforcement. This tension sits at the intersection of student conduct and faculty accountability. Students recognize that punctuality, device use, and preparation are their responsibilities, but they also see enforcement as a faculty responsibility. When professors don't follow through on stated expectations, the norms lose meaning. The disconnect is sharpest in comparisons with HBS, where joint-degree students describe a culture of consistent consequences that HKS lacks. Students are not asking for draconian rules. They are asking for clarity about what is actually expected and consistency in how those expectations are upheld.
norms-enforcement.whats_working: Students generally appreciate when professors set clear expectations on day one. Several noted that the best classroom experiences came from professors who were explicit about norms and followed through consistently.
norms-enforcement.areas_for_improvement: Enforcement is inconsistent across classes. Some professors call out tardiness and phone use; others ignore it entirely. Students describe confusion about what the 'real' rules are versus the stated ones. Joint-degree students with HBS experience describe the contrast as stark.

curated_quotes.text: If someone walks in late, the teacher should say, this is your warning. The next class, get out. You're late. It's just establishing that if you cross this line, there's going to be a repercussion. The problem is that most lines at the Kennedy School, when you cross them, there's no repercussions.
curated_quotes.note: Joint-degree student comparing to HBS

curated_quotes.text: Classes should start on time. Teachers should be ready five to ten minutes before. The norm should be that everyone is on time. The norm is that people aren't on their laptops in the back. I think less than 25% of the people on their computers in a Kennedy School class are actually taking notes.
curated_quotes.note: On device culture

curated_quotes.text: I think the spoken rules always sound super reasonable and illegitimate. But behind those external rules, there are also implied rules that everyone understands what they are, but no one mentions them.
curated_quotes.note: On the gap between stated and actual norms

curated_quotes.text: I would definitely be keeping an eye out to see if the professor was treating everyone the same way. If anyone got a pass on this type of behavior, I'd see it much more negatively. Whereas if a professor is treating everyone the exact same way, and expectations were set clearly on the syllabus, I don't think I'd have a problem with it.
curated_quotes.note: Fairness and consistency matter more than strictness

curated_quotes.text: There is a certain merit to holding people to a certain academic standard. I genuinely feel that we should all be collectively holding ourselves to a better preparation for class. On one hand, I don't want other people to be late or underprepared. On the other hand, I don't want people to be intimidated.
curated_quotes.note: Tension between standards and psychological safety

curated_quotes.text: For sure. But if there's this rule that we shouldn't be on technology, is it a rule? It's not a rule. You know what I mean?
curated_quotes.note: When unenforced rules aren't really rules

norms-enforcement.discussion_question: Should HKS establish school-wide baseline expectations for classroom conduct (punctuality, device use, preparedness) that professors can tighten but not loosen? What would enforcement look like in practice?

cold-calling.label: Cold Calling
cold-calling.description: Cold calling generated genuinely split opinion, not along program lines but along pedagogical philosophy lines. Supporters see it as professionally relevant preparation for being put on the spot. Critics worry about its impact when overused or when it becomes the entire class dynamic rather than one tool among many. The nuance matters: students are not rejecting cold calling outright. They are asking for it to be deployed thoughtfully, with adequate warning about class format in syllabi.
cold-calling.whats_working: When cold calling is used as one tool among several, students find it sharpens preparation and mirrors professional settings. Several praised 'warm calling' (advance notice) as effective.
cold-calling.areas_for_improvement: Some students described dropping classes because cold calling dominated the entire pedagogy. Others noted that cold calling in very large classes (80+) creates anxiety without the benefit of genuine discussion. The key request: syllabi should clearly signal the extent of cold calling so students can make informed enrollment decisions.

curated_quotes.text: I dropped a class because of cold calling. The class that I really waited for, because the professor was doing cold calling in such a way that it was the whole essence of the class.
curated_quotes.note: When cold calling drives away engaged students

curated_quotes.text: I'm not against cold calling. I just think that sometimes if it's the whole essence of the class, maybe the syllabus should mention that.
curated_quotes.note: The ask is for transparency, not abolition

curated_quotes.text: Cold calling as a general thing is great. I think it can really enhance learning. But it's a spectrum. If you go to the other extreme where the focus is to just put people on the spot, that's different.
curated_quotes.note: Support for cold calling with limits

curated_quotes.text: I think cold calling, in my undergrad we actually don't have a lot of cold calling, because the class size is really large. So because at HKS the class size is smaller, I think it works.
curated_quotes.note: Class size determines effectiveness

curated_quotes.text: She was warm calling, and it was on reading. It would be in the beginning of class. And I thought it was effective because it held people accountable for doing the reading.
curated_quotes.note: Warm calling as a middle ground

cold-calling.discussion_question: Should course descriptions or syllabi be required to indicate the extent of cold calling and participation expectations, so students can make informed enrollment choices?

feedback-assessment.label: Feedback & Assessment: Timing, Quality, and Accountability
feedback-assessment.description: Assignment feedback emerged as one of the strongest themes across programs. Students describe a system with enormous variance: some professors provide detailed, timely feedback while others return grades weeks late with minimal comments, sometimes delegated entirely to CAs. The frustration is not just about speed. It is about the educational compact. Students who invest heavily in assignments feel shortchanged when feedback does not help them improve. The structural issue is clear: there are few school-wide standards for feedback timing or quality.
feedback-assessment.whats_working: Several students praised individual professors who provide detailed, thoughtful feedback. One MCMPA student specifically valued knowing a professor (not a TA) read every assignment, even if it took longer. The J-term course 'Being Human' was cited as a model for layered feedback from both professor and TA.
feedback-assessment.areas_for_improvement: Feedback timing is unpredictable. One student reported not receiving a single grade back the entire semester in two classes. Course evaluations are due before grades are returned, undermining the feedback loop. Students want clearer expectations about what feedback to expect and when, even if it varies by class.

curated_quotes.text: I find it odd that there aren't more rules or structures around what professors can and can't do around assessment structure, around feedback expectations, timing. I feel like every class you go to, it's kind of a random gamble.
curated_quotes.note: Desire for structural consistency

curated_quotes.text: I had two classes last semester that I didn't get a single grade back the entire semester. I got A's in both the classes.
curated_quotes.note: Grades without feedback defeats the purpose

curated_quotes.text: I've had a very different experience. Not the timeline, but knowing that the instructor or professor will be reading every assignment and not a TA. I'm willing to wait that period so I get that full feedback. Very detailed feedback.
curated_quotes.note: Quality can compensate for speed

curated_quotes.text: We're expected to submit reviews of the professors before we even get our grades back at the end of the semester. I think that this is very typical.
curated_quotes.note: Student sees this timing problem as common, not exceptional

curated_quotes.text: One suggestion for the professor would be to just share a detailed rubric and a model answer. That's worked well in the courses that we've had them.
curated_quotes.note: Concrete solution from students

curated_quotes.text: There are professors who have gotten feedback returned quickly, but sometimes it's clear that their CAs or TFs are doing the gradings and not them, and that makes a difference.
curated_quotes.note: Students notice who actually reads their work

feedback-assessment.discussion_question: Should HKS establish minimum standards for feedback timing (e.g., grades returned before course evaluations are due) and require syllabi to specify the feedback structure?

teaching-quality.label: Teaching Quality & Faculty Investment
teaching-quality.description: Students distinguish clearly between the best and worst teaching experiences at HKS, and the gap is wide. The best professors are described as deeply prepared, pedagogically intentional, and invested in student learning. But quality is inconsistent, and students want to understand what incentives and structures exist to hold teaching quality accountable. The question of how HKS evaluates and develops its professors came up explicitly.
teaching-quality.whats_working: Faculty are broadly seen as professional and knowledgeable. Multiple students described individual professors as 'deeply inspiring' in their preparation and pedagogical design. The MPAID program received especially strong praise for interconnecting courses and managing discussions effectively.
teaching-quality.areas_for_improvement: There is wide variability across professors. Some appear to have designed courses around their research interests rather than student learning outcomes. Students want more pedagogical investment and wonder whether HKS has mechanisms to address teaching quality, particularly for discussion facilitation, which many professors handle poorly.

curated_quotes.text: My experience with my professors here has been deeply inspiring. No matter whatever priorities they had, they treated me, their students, as their top priority.
curated_quotes.note: Faculty investment at its best

curated_quotes.text: How does HKS assess professors? What are the incentives, and what are the performance mechanisms? Because I can see instances where there are amazing professors, but probably there's something to be learned when professors are not as strong.
curated_quotes.note: Asking about accountability structures

curated_quotes.text: From a professionalism standpoint, HKS is head and shoulders above the design school, where nobody pays attention in class whatsoever.
curated_quotes.note: Favorable comparison from HGSD dual degree

curated_quotes.text: When I arrived at HKS and was told that we'd be doing case discussions, I had a different expectation than what I received in most of my classes.
curated_quotes.note: Gap between promise and delivery on case method

curated_quotes.text: They really reflected on what it means to learn. You can see it in the way that they teach.
curated_quotes.note: Pedagogical intentionality

curated_quotes.text: All the teachers try to connect what you learn in one class into another one and try to make everything practical as you go through your entire degree.
curated_quotes.note: MPAID faculty praised for cross-course coherence

teaching-quality.discussion_question: What mechanisms currently exist for faculty teaching development at HKS, and are they sufficient to address the quality variance students describe?

office-hours.label: Faculty Accessibility & Office Hours
office-hours.description: Office hours surfaced as a concrete access point where structural constraints become visible. Large class sizes mean limited slots. Some professors open office hours to any HKS student, diluting access for enrolled students. Scheduling friction (inconsistent platforms, limited windows) compounds the problem. Students frame this as a professional relationship issue: they want more than transactional Q&A sessions.
office-hours.whats_working: Some professors are described as deeply accessible and responsive, even when busy. Students appreciate direct email access and flexibility in scheduling.
office-hours.areas_for_improvement: Limited office hour slots for large classes. Inconsistent booking platforms create confusion. Some students feel office hours should prioritize enrolled students. One student called accessibility 'a core performance metric' for professors.

curated_quotes.text: Accessibility towards students should be a core performance metric for teachers. It's unacceptable that there are some professors who are saying, I only have one office hour a week for a class of 60 students.
curated_quotes.note: Structural mismatch between class size and access

curated_quotes.text: The office hours are open for everyone, even students who don't take the professor's class. So the student can probably find a time, but that means fewer slots for enrolled students.
curated_quotes.note: Open access dilutes availability

curated_quotes.text: Consistent formatting for office hours would help. I have had a professor who used Calendly, and I didn't realize they updated every two weeks.
curated_quotes.note: Small friction points add up

curated_quotes.text: It's all about the expectations. A lot of students expect coaching feedback, but it's fair to say office hours is a better venue for coaching than writing up a paragraph on an assignment.
curated_quotes.note: Realistic about what feedback channels can deliver

office-hours.discussion_question: Should there be minimum office hour requirements scaled to class size, and should booking be standardized across courses?

readings-workload.label: Reading Volume & Workload Sustainability
readings-workload.description: Students across programs (especially MCMPAs and MPP1s) describe reading volumes that are unrealistic and, crucially, often disconnected from what happens in class. The frustration is not with hard work. It is with work that feels pointless when professors do not draw on assigned readings during sessions. MPAID students, by contrast, praised their program office's deliberate workload management as a model.
readings-workload.whats_working: The MPAID program office actively manages the workload calendar across courses to prevent assignment pile-ups. Students described this as transformative for their learning experience.
readings-workload.areas_for_improvement: Some courses assign 200 to 400 pages per week with no accountability for having read them. Students want depth over volume, and they want readings to connect to class discussions. Course packets should be available before enrollment for informed course selection.

curated_quotes.text: Reduce the volume of work. Not necessarily assignments, but the readings. I feel like I'm getting such a surface-level understanding of so much, and I'm not getting a deep understanding of anything.
curated_quotes.note: Breadth over depth frustration

curated_quotes.text: There are some professors where it's 400 pages of readings for one class, and you're like, okay, well, what is the point of this?
curated_quotes.note: Volume without purpose

curated_quotes.text: It would be very helpful if before we are starting a course, we can get our course packets. That happens in HLS. That happens in HBS.
curated_quotes.note: Pre-enrollment materials as standard at peer schools

curated_quotes.text: There should be a meeting for arranging volume of reading among professors. Last semester, one of my classes gave me 200 pages per week.
curated_quotes.note: No cross-course coordination

curated_quotes.text: The program office manages the workload calendar. They really put a lot of thought into it and make sure that we don't have too many assignments due in one week. That really helps a lot in the learning culture overall.
curated_quotes.note: MPAID's workload management as a model

readings-workload.discussion_question: Should professors be required to coordinate reading loads across courses in a given semester, similar to MPAID's workload calendar model?

rigor-program-impressions.label: Academic Rigor: Expectations Met and Unmet
rigor-program-impressions.description: Rigor is the theme that most sharply divides along program lines. MPAID students find it appropriately challenging and well-designed. MPP1s describe it as 'extremely underwhelming' with inconsistent standards. MCMPAs appreciate the democratic classroom culture but see discussions as sometimes performative rather than substantive. The common thread: rigor is not a simple dial. Students want the right level of challenge, clearly signaled expectations, and accountability for both preparation and engagement.
rigor-program-impressions.whats_working: MPAID students are the most satisfied with rigor, praising both the challenge level and the coherence across courses. MCMPAs value the openness and democratic nature of HKS classroom culture compared to prior educational experiences. Several students across programs noted strong individual courses and professors.
rigor-program-impressions.areas_for_improvement: The heterogeneity of student preparation creates a leveling problem: some students find courses too easy, others too hard, and the middle is unsatisfying for both. Large participation grades in large classes produce quantity over quality in discussions. Some students describe being 'spoon-fed' administratively in ways that undermine professional development.

curated_quotes.text: I think it oftentimes exceeded my expectations in terms of rigor and also coherence between the different classes. I've been really impressed by the rigor, maybe too much at times where the pace has been difficult to manage.
curated_quotes.note: MPAID positive experience

curated_quotes.text: When it comes to professionalism, I think HKS is very high, in a positive way. When it comes to rigor, I would say it's extremely underwhelming.
curated_quotes.note: Professionalism-rigor disconnect

curated_quotes.text: The fact that no one really uses their phones, everyone is paying attention, almost everyone comes prepared. In fact, there is the social pressure that if you don't prepare, you'll be found out, which I think is great.
curated_quotes.note: Positive take on peer accountability

curated_quotes.text: People should fail more classes. There's this very strong aversion in the culture to people being able to fail. Graduating students who put in very little effort damages the brand.
curated_quotes.note: Standards and consequences

curated_quotes.text: So the way of teaching is very different from what we have back home. It's more liberal and democratic in terms of how the class is conducted. And the openness of it, I think that's very positive.
curated_quotes.note: International student valuing HKS approach

curated_quotes.text: Accommodating to the point of low expectations.
curated_quotes.note: Two-word summary of the rigor concern

rigor-program-impressions.discussion_question: How can HKS maintain inclusive classroom culture while also raising the floor on intellectual rigor, particularly in discussion management and grading accountability?

participation-class-size.label: Participation Grades vs. Class Size: A Structural Tension
participation-class-size.description: This is one of the clearest structural findings: high participation grades (40 to 50%) in large classes (80 to 90 students) create perverse incentives. Students feel pressure to speak for the sake of being counted rather than to advance discussion. The result is lower-quality contributions, less airtime per student, and a dynamic where quantity crowds out depth. Students are not asking for smaller participation grades in small seminars. The problem is specifically the interaction between large enrollment and heavy participation weighting.
participation-class-size.whats_working: In smaller classes and seminars, participation grading works well and mirrors professional norms. MPAID students praised how their professors manage participation and encourage meaningful engagement. Some professors use teaching tools that track contributions without relying on hand-raising.
participation-class-size.areas_for_improvement: Classes of 70 to 90 students with 40 to 50% participation grades create a structural impossibility: meaningful discussion among that many people. Students describe it as disruptive and performative. Several also questioned whether tracking tools (like 'Teachly') measure quality or just frequency.

curated_quotes.text: Classes way too big. 80-90 people, and a 40 to 50 percent participation grade. People feel like they need to talk, but you can't have a conversation amongst a hundred people.
curated_quotes.note: The core structural tension

curated_quotes.text: I think it's an intersection of class size and a huge participation grade. It really incentivizes people to speak for the sake of having their name noted rather than to advance the discussion.
curated_quotes.note: Perverse incentive

curated_quotes.text: It's also Teachly, from my understanding it tracks how many times you participate, which is a ridiculous measure of the quality of your contributions.
curated_quotes.note: Quantity over quality in tracking

curated_quotes.text: If you're going to have classes that large, you can't have a sizable participation grade. Or make the whole class for that day a discussion, like how it is at HBS.
curated_quotes.note: Concrete alternative proposed

curated_quotes.text: We need to reduce class sizes. The size of the race and racism class makes me feel like the program doesn't actually care about race and racism.
curated_quotes.note: Class size as a signal about institutional priorities

curated_quotes.text: I noticed that there's not much disagreement with what students are saying, even if something might be factually incorrect or questionable. If basic inaccuracy is allowed to stand in a classroom, you're robbing that person of the opportunity to learn.
curated_quotes.note: Lack of intellectual pushback in discussions

participation-class-size.discussion_question: Should HKS set guidelines for participation grade weighting relative to class size (e.g., capping participation at 20% for classes above 50 students)?

core-curriculum.label: Core Curriculum: Structure, Flexibility, and Program Identity
core-curriculum.description: Core curriculum is the theme that most clearly splits along degree lines. MPP students with a large required core want more flexibility and leveling. MPA dual-degree students with almost no core want more structure and coherence. MPAID students are broadly satisfied but want their core updated to reflect the evolving field. The shared request across all groups: let the core build toward something intentional, not just check boxes. Notably, MPP1s (currently navigating core requirements) express more frustration than MPP2s (who have more distance from the experience), suggesting that sentiment about the core may shift over the course of the degree.
core-curriculum.whats_working: The MPAID core is praised for coherence, with courses that connect to each other and build sequentially. The MPP core's negotiations course and some economics tracks are valued. Joint-degree students who have a structured pathway (like MPP/HBS) describe their degree as intentional and well-directed.
core-curriculum.areas_for_improvement: MPP1s want core requirements to accommodate different preparation levels. Advanced students get stuck in introductory courses they have already mastered. MPA dual-degree students describe a 'hodgepodge' of classes with no coherent throughline. Multiple students want the core redesigned around professional functions and skills rather than academic topics. MPAID students want more U.S. development content alongside international.

curated_quotes.text: It's hard to have intentionality when you don't have any core. Most people actually don't know where they're going and they end up with a hodgepodge of classes that don't really align in any way.
curated_quotes.note: MPA dual degree student on having too little structure

curated_quotes.text: We have too much core. I think that my degree feels very intentional. I know exactly what I'm doing.
curated_quotes.note: MPP/HBS joint student, by contrast, has clear direction because of structured requirements

curated_quotes.text: When people say get rid of core classes, what they really mean is adjust for different learning levels. A degree has to have core requirements, but more optionality within core, adjusted to learning levels, is key.
curated_quotes.note: Not anti-core, but pro-leveling

curated_quotes.text: We need to stop thinking about topics and start thinking about functions. If we were to have an end-to-end workflow of something that a government does, what are the skills that I need? There needs to be a finance and budgeting class. There should be an operations class. There should be a leadership class.
curated_quotes.note: Skills-based core redesign: build around professional functions, not academic departments

curated_quotes.text: The MPA/ID needs to be rethought. Some of these classes have not been restructured in 25 years.
curated_quotes.note: Even the praised program needs updating

curated_quotes.text: If people who are more advanced can opt into more difficult courses, then the Core can adjust to meet the needs of students who are struggling. One of the challenges is people's questions aren't being answered enough in stats or econ.
curated_quotes.note: Leveling as a solution to mixed preparation

core-curriculum.discussion_question: HKS already has some pilot efforts around tracks and demonstrated competency. Should these be expanded, deepened, or restructured? Specifically, should the core be reorganized around professional functions and skills (e.g., budgeting, operations, strategy) rather than academic disciplines?

professionalism-student.label: Student Professionalism & Classroom Culture
professionalism-student.description: When asked about 'professionalism,' students interpret the term in two distinct ways: classroom conduct (behavior, punctuality, device use) and career preparation (whether the degree is making them job-ready). This mirrors the bidirectional definition that motivated these focus groups, where professionalism applies to both student responsibility and institutional responsibility. On conduct, MPAID students are most positive; joint-degree students with HBS experience are most critical. On career readiness, MCMPAs express the most concern. The key insight is that professionalism is not just about individual behavior. It is shaped by the incentives, norms, and enforcement structures the institution creates.
professionalism-student.whats_working: MPAID students describe classroom conduct as 'very professional.' Multiple students across programs note a culture of respect and attentiveness in their best courses. Professors who set clear norms on day one create the conditions for professional behavior.
professionalism-student.areas_for_improvement: Joint-degree students describe an HKS 'professionalism problem' relative to HBS. Some MCMPAs doubt whether their degree is making them job-ready. The definition of professionalism itself is contested. Students want clarity about whether HKS sees itself as a professional school with professional-school norms.

curated_quotes.text: About student conduct in class, I think that's very professional.
curated_quotes.note: MPAID's positive baseline

curated_quotes.text: At the end of the day it's all about the professor's leadership that makes that class good.
curated_quotes.note: Faculty set the tone

curated_quotes.text: I think the professors are quite engaging. But oftentimes there's one or two people who take up the entirety of the class. In 75 percent of my classes, I've experienced this.
curated_quotes.note: Discussion domination problem

curated_quotes.text: Competitive. And it depends on professor.
curated_quotes.note: Two-word summary of MPP1 classroom culture

curated_quotes.text: I don't know if I can say I am a public administration professional.
curated_quotes.note: MPA dual degree questioning career readiness

professionalism-student.discussion_question: Should HKS articulate an explicit institutional definition of 'professional classroom culture' that goes beyond individual course syllabi?

noise_explanation: Clusters 0 (voting exercise mechanics), 3 (introductions), and 4 (conversational filler) are excluded.
